Michael Jeffrey Jordan was born on February 17, 1963.
Michael Jeffrey Jordan is also known by his initials MJ.
Jordan played college basketball with the North Carolina Tar Heels.
Jordan was a member of the Tar Heels' national championship team in 1982 as a freshman.
Jordan joined the Bulls in 1984 as the third overall draft pick.
Jordan quickly emerged as a league star, entertaining crowds with his prolific scoring while gaining a reputation as one of the best defensive players.
Jordan performed slam dunks from the free-throw line during Slam Dunk Contests, earning him the nicknames "Air Jordan" and "His Airness".
Jordan won his first NBA title with the Bulls in 1991.
Jordan followed that achievement with titles in 1992 and 1993, securing a three-peat.
Jordan abruptly retired from basketball before the 1993–94 NBA season to play Minor League Baseball in the Chicago White Sox organization.
Jordan returned to the Bulls in March 1995 and led them to three more championships in 1996, 1997, and 1998.
Jordan was selected to play for the United States national team during his college and NBA careers.
Jordan won four gold medals at the 1983 Pan American Games, 1984 Summer Olympics, 1992 Tournament of the Americas, and 1992 Summer Olympics.
Jordan was named the greatest basketball player of the 20th century by the Associated Press.
Jordan was named the greatest North American athlete of the 20th century by ESPN.

Jordan was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame twice: once for his individual career and again as part of the 1992 United States men's Olympic basketball team ("The Dream Team").
Jordan became a member of the United States Olympic Hall of Fame in 2009.
Jordan was named to the NBA 50th Anniversary Team in 1996.
Jordan was named to the NBA 75th Anniversary Team in 2021.
Jordan's individual accolades include six NBA Finals Most Valuable Player (MVP) awards, ten NBA scoring titles, five NBA MVP awards, and so on.
Jordan is one of only seven players in history to win six NBA Finals playing for one team with the Bulls.
Jordan was born at Cumberland Hospital in Brooklyn, New York City.
Jordan's siblings include two older brothers, James Jr. and Larry, as well as an older sister named Deloris and a younger sister named Roslyn.
The family moved to Wilmington, North Carolina, in 1968.
Jordan attended Emsley A. Laney High School.
Jordan tried out for the basketball varsity team during his sophomore year but was deemed too short at 5 feet 11 inches (1.80 m).
Jordan became the star of Laney's junior varsity team and tallied some 40-point games after growing four inches in height.
Upon earning a spot on the varsity roster, Jordan averaged more than 25 points per game over his final two seasons of high school play.
Jordan was selected to play in the 1981 McDonald's All-American Game as a senior and scored 30 points.
Jordan accepted a basketball scholarship to the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.
Jordan majored in cultural geography while at UNC.
Jordan chose this field of study because of its relationship to meteorology, as Jordan was interested in a career as a meteorologist.
Jordan was named ACC Freshman of the Year after averaging 13.4 ppg on 53.4% shooting (field goal percentage).
Jordan made the game-winning jump shot in the 1982 NCAA Championship game against Georgetown.
Jordan left North Carolina a year before his scheduled graduation to enter the 1984 NBA draft.
Jordan returned to North Carolina to complete his degree in 1986, graduating with a Bachelor of Arts degree in geography.
The Chicago Bulls selected Jordan with the third overall pick of the 1984 NBA draft after Hakeem Olajuwon and Sam Bowie.
Jordan made his NBA debut at Chicago Stadium on October 26, 1984, scoring 16 points.
During his rookie 1984–85 season with the Bulls, Jordan averaged 28.2 ppg on 51.5% shooting.
Jordan's 1985–86 season was cut short when he broke his foot in the third game of the year, missing 64 games.
The Bulls finished the season 38–44 and lost to the Milwaukee Bucks in four games in the first round of the playoffs.
On August 26, 1985, Jordan shattered the glass of the backboard with a dunk during an exhibition game in Trieste, Italy.
Jordan's 1985–86 season was cut short when he broke his foot in the third game of the year.
The Bulls made the playoffs despite Jordan's injury and a 30–52 record, at the time the fifth-worst record of any team to qualify for the playoffs in NBA history.
Jordan recovered in time to participate in the postseason and performed well upon his return.
On April 20 at the Boston Garden, in Game 2 of the First Round, Jordan scored a playoff career-high 63 points, breaking Elgin Baylor's single-game playoff scoring record.
The Bulls finished with a 47–35 record and advanced to the Eastern Conference Finals for the first time in Jordan's career.
In the Eastern Conference Semifinals, the Bulls lost in five games to the Detroit Pistons led by Isiah Thomas and known as the "Bad Boys".
Jordan led the league in scoring during the 1987–88 season, averaging 35.0 ppg on 53.5% shooting.
Jordan was named the NBA Defensive Player of the Year after averaging 1.6 blocks per game (bpg), a league-high 3.1 steals per game (spg).
The Bulls finished 50–32 and made it past the first round of the playoffs for the first time in Jordan's career.
Jordan led the league in scoring during the 1987–88 season, averaging 35.0 ppg on 53.5% shooting from the field.
The Bulls defeated the New York Knicks and the Philadelphia 76ers in the opening two rounds of the playoffs.
They advanced to the Eastern Conference Finals where they lost in six games to the Detroit Pistons.
Jordan was selected by consensus to the NCAA All-American First Team in both his sophomore (1983) and junior (1984) seasons.
Jordan's 1985–86 season was cut short when he broke his foot in the third game of the year, missing 64 games.
The Bulls entered the 1989–90 season as a team on the rise with their core group of Jordan and young improving players like Scottie Pippen and Horace Grant.
On March 28, 1990, Jordan scored a career-high 69 points in a 117–113 road win over the Cavaliers.
Jordan won his second MVP award after averaging 31.5 ppg on 53.9% shooting, 6.0 rpg, and 5.5 apg for the regular season.
The Bulls finished in first place in their division for the first time in sixteen years with a 61–21 record.
The Bulls defeated the New York Knicks and the Philadelphia 76ers in the opening two rounds of the playoffs.
They advanced to the Eastern Conference Finals where they lost in six games to the Detroit Pistons.
Jordan was named NBA Most Valuable Player for the second year in a row with averages of 30.1 ppg, 6.4 rpg, and 6.1 apg on 52% shooting.
The Bulls won the series in five games against the Los Angeles Lakers, who had Magic Johnson and James Worthy as formidable opponents.
Jordan scored more than 30 points in every game of the series, including 40 or more points in four consecutive games.
Jordan was named Finals MVP for the second year in a row with averages of 35.8 ppg, 4.8 rpg, and 6.5 apg.
Jordan announced his retirement on October 6, 1993, saying he lost his desire to play basketball.
The murder of Jordan's father three months earlier helped shape his decision.
James R. Jordan Sr. was murdered on July 23, 1993, at a highway rest area in Lumberton, North Carolina, by two teenagers, Daniel Green and Larry Martin Demery.
Green and Demery were sentenced to life imprisonment for the murder of James R. Jordan Sr.
Jordan signed a Minor League Baseball (MiLB) contract with the Chicago White Sox on February 7, 1994.
Jordan reported to spring training in Sarasota, Florida, and was assigned to the team's minor league system on March 31.

Jordan played for the Birmingham Barons, a Double-A minor league affiliate of the Chicago White Sox, batting .202 with three home runs, 51 RBIs, 30 stolen bases, 114 strikeouts, 51 walks, and 11 errors.
Jordan also appeared for the Scottsdale Scorpions in the 1994 Arizona Fall League, batting .252 against top prospects in baseball.
On November 1, 1994, his No. 23 was retired by the Bulls in a ceremony that included the erection of a permanent sculpture known as The Spirit outside the new United Center.
The Bulls went 55–27 in 1993–94 without Jordan and lost to the New York Knicks in the second round of the playoffs.
Jordan decided to quit baseball because he feared becoming a replacement player during the Major League Baseball strike.
On March 18, 1995, Jordan announced his return to the NBA with two-word press release: "I'm back."
The next day, Jordan took to the court with the Bulls to face the Indiana Pacers in Indianapolis, scoring 19 points.
Despite his 18-month hiatus from the NBA, Jordan played well, making a game-winning jump shot against Atlanta in his fourth game back.
Jordan scored 55 points in his next game, against the New York Knicks at Madison Square Garden on March 28, 1995.
Boosted by Jordan's comeback, the Bulls went 13–4 to make the playoffs and advanced to the Eastern Conference Semifinals against the Orlando Magic.
At the end of Game 1, Orlando's Nick Anderson stripped Jordan from behind, leading to the game-winning basket for the Magic.
Jordan responded by scoring 38 points in the next game, which Chicago won.
Before the game, Jordan decided that he would immediately resume wearing his former No. 23.
The Bulls were fined $25,000 for failing to report the impromptu number change to the NBA.
Jordan was fined an additional $5,000 for opting to wear white sneakers when the rest of the Bulls wore black.
Jordan averaged 31 ppg in the playoffs but Orlando won the series in six games.
The Bulls went 72–10 during the 1995–96 season with Jordan leading the league in scoring with 30.4 ppg and winning the league's regular season MVP award.

The Bulls lost only three games in four series (Miami Heat 3–0, New York Knicks 4–1, and Orlando Magic 4–0) as they defeated the Seattle SuperSonics 4–2 in the NBA Finals to win their fourth championship.
Jordan was named Finals MVP for a record fourth time; he achieved only the second sweep of the MVP awards in the All-Star Game, regular season, and NBA Finals after Willis Reed in the 1969–70 season.
Upon winning the championship, his first since his father's murder, Jordan reacted emotionally, clutching the game ball and crying on the locker room floor.
In the 1996–97 season, the Bulls stood at a 69–11 record but ended the year with a final two games loss to finish the year 69–13.
The Bulls again advanced to the Finals where they faced the Utah Jazz.
That team included Karl Malone who had beaten Jordan for the NBA MVP award in a tight race (986–957).
In Game 1, Jordan won with a buzzer-beating jump shot.
In Game 5, despite being feverish and dehydrated from a stomach virus, Jordan played and scored 38 points including the game-winning three-pointer with 25 seconds remaining.
The Bulls won 90–88 and went on to win the series in six games. For the fifth time in as many Finals appearances, Jordan received the Finals MVP award for a record sixth time.
During the 1997 NBA All-Star Game, he posted the first triple-double in All-Star Game history but the MVP award went to Glen Rice.
The Bulls compiled a 62–20 record during the 1997–98 season with Jordan leading the league with 28.7 ppg and securing his fifth regular season MVP award.
Jordan was named to the NBA 50th Anniversary Team in 1996 and to the NBA 75th Anniversary Team in 2021.
The trophy for the NBA Most Valuable Player Award is named in Jordan's honor.
One of the most effectively marketed athletes of his generation, Jordan made many product endorsements.
He fueled the success of Nike's Air Jordan sneakers which were introduced in 1984 and remain popular.
Jordan starred as himself in the live-action/animation hybrid film Space Jam (1996) and was the central focus of the Emmy-winning documentary series The Last Dance (2020).
